title: Who should print first?
hook: The same four jobs, the same printer. Does the order change how long everyone waits?

knows: a queue serves jobs one at a time (back-button-stack)
doesNotKnow: that the order of jobs changes the total waiting

misconception: The total time people spend waiting is the same whatever order the jobs run in.
objective: The learner can explain that a job at the front delays every job behind it, so running 8, 4, 2, 1 longest first gives a total wait of 34 minutes and shortest first gives 11; and that shortest first can starve a long job.

claims.text: Run longest first (8, 4, 2, 1 minutes), the jobs wait 0 + 8 + 12 + 14 = 34 minutes in total.
claims.source: Each job waits for the sum of the jobs before it. Checked in node by the builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): 0 + 8 + 12 + 14 = 34 (node).

claims.text: Shortest first (1, 2, 4, 8), the total wait is 0 + 1 + 3 + 7 = 11 minutes, about a third of 34.
claims.source: Arithmetic; 11/34 = 0.32. Checked in node by the builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): 0 + 1 + 3 + 7 = 11; 11/34 = 0.324 (node). Over all 24 orders min 11, max 34.

claims.text: A job at the front makes every job behind it wait, so its length counts once for each job behind it; shortest first gives the smallest total wait.
claims.source: Total wait = sum over positions of duration x (jobs behind it); exchange argument. Smith, 'Various optimizers for single-stage production', Naval Research Logistics Quarterly 3 (1956): shortest processing time first minimises total completion time on one machine. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Exchange argument re-derived: total wait = sum of d_i x (jobs behind i), minimised by sorting ascending. Smith, NRLQ 3(1-2):59-66 (1956), single-machine total completion time = total wait + fixed sum of durations.

claims.text: If short jobs keep arriving, a long job can wait forever under shortest first.
claims.source: If a new shorter job is always waiting when the machine frees up, the long job is never chosen (starvation). Silberschatz, Galvin, Gagne, Operating System Concepts, CPU scheduling chapter (SJF and starvation). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Starvation under non-preemptive SJF with continual short arrivals; Silberschatz et al., CPU scheduling.

recall.question: Three customers need 10, 1 and 1 minutes at one counter. To make their total waiting time as small as possible, who goes first?
options: The 10-minute customer, to get it over with
recall.why: The first job's length is added to every wait behind it. 1, 1, 10 gives waits 0 + 1 + 2 = 3; 10 first gives 0 + 10 + 11 = 21.
